content.text:
I submitted **part-based**, with confidence 0.85. I used 48 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L2-S2-M2. I then tested tasks where the number of new rules and the output similarity to the trained tasks (from `compare`) point in opposite directions. Results were very noisy (single tests ranged from 1 to 67 examples), so I repeated each test 6 to 13 times.

| Test task | New rules | Highest output overlap with a trained task | Mean examples to criterion (n) |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M2 | 0 | 0.375 | 16.1 (13) |
| L2-S1-M2 | 0 | 0.625 | 16.7 (6) |
| L1-S3-M1 | 1 | 0.625 | 27.0 (6) |
| L4-S4-M4 | 3 | 0.5625 | 32.0 (13) |
| L3-S3-M3 | 3 | ~0.06 | 41.8 (8) |

**Why part-based:**
- **Key comparison:** L4-S4-M4 has no rules in common with the trained tasks but overlaps more with them in output, yet it took about twice as many examples as L1-S1-M2 (t ≈ 3.4).
- **Similarity didn't matter when rules were known:** the two tasks made only of known rules cost about the same, even though their overlap differs a lot (0.375 vs 0.625).
- **Cost followed new-rule count:** cost rose step by step with the number of new rules (about 16, then 27, then 35).

**Main caveat:** the holistic learner's similarity measure is hidden. If it happens to track shared rules rather than shared outputs, it could produce this same pattern, which is why the confidence isn't higher.
